what_it_is.body: Monad is a new general-purpose Layer 1 that runs Ethereum bytecode and RPC tooling without settling to Ethereum. MonadBFT orders blocks, while asynchronous and parallel execution, JIT compilation and MonadDb are designed to increase throughput. This is an independent validator network, not an Ethereum rollup, so its security, liquidity and economics stand on their own.

what_happened.body: Public mainnet launched on November 24, 2025. By this review Monad held $770.87 million of TVL, $620.81 million of dollar stablecoins and $1.29 billion of thirty-day DEX volume. TVL was only 7.52% below its July 31 peak, but MON traded at $0.0217, 55.58% below its recorded high, and its $2.18 billion fully diluted value was far above its $256.55 million circulating market value.

why_this_outcome.body: Monad removed a real adoption cost: Solidity teams can reuse familiar contracts and tools while seeking faster execution. Large financing, Foundation grants and unlocked ecosystem tokens helped seed applications and liquidity quickly. That explains the strong launch footprint, but it also makes organic demand hard to isolate. The chain is too young to know whether users remain after incentives, and the token market is already pricing substantial future supply.

strategic_choices.body: Monad chose a sovereign L1 instead of an Ethereum L2, preserved EVM compatibility, rewrote the client stack for performance and raised $225 million before mainnet. At token launch, roughly 38.5% of MON was unlocked for Foundation-managed ecosystem development while team and investor allocations began with one-year locks. These choices accelerated distribution and gave the chain economic control, while concentrating execution risk in a young client stack and future supply decisions.

operating_model.body: Validators stake MON and participate in MonadBFT. The protocol pipelines consensus and execution, then executes compatible transactions in parallel while preserving Ethereum-style results. Category Labs built the first consensus and execution clients, and the Foundation coordinates ecosystem programs and delegation. Validator, client and delegation diversity therefore matter as much as headline throughput.

token_and_value_capture.body: MON pays gas, is delegated to validators and receives block rewards. Base transaction fees burn, while each successful block mints 25 MON; the launch documents estimated about 2 billion MON of annual inflation before burns. The initial supply was 100 billion. Because only part of that supply circulates, activity can grow while holders still absorb rewards, Foundation deployment and scheduled team and investor releases.

counterfactual.body: Launching as an Ethereum L2 could have reduced validator cold-start risk and provided Ethereum settlement, but it would have weakened Monad’s sovereignty and performance thesis. A smaller ecosystem allocation or slower subsidy program would yield a cleaner test of organic demand, while likely slowing launch growth. Neither alternative guarantees applications would choose Monad over established EVM and non-EVM chains.

risks_and_unknowns.body: The central risks are incentive-dependent liquidity, a young production codebase, validator or infrastructure concentration, shared-state performance under real contention and the large gap between circulating and diluted token value. Aggregate TVL and volume do not identify repeat users. We lack an independent entity map for validators, a subsidy-adjusted application cohort and a reconciled schedule of actual Foundation token deployment.

lifecycle.body: Monad is mixed because it has real early liquidity and trading but too little history for a durable success call. TVL remains close to its peak and thirty-day volume is meaningful. Against that, MON is 55.58% below its high, circulating value is a small fraction of diluted value, and Foundation-managed ecosystem capital can blur whether demand is earned or rented. This is a promising launch, not yet a proven moat.

outlook_and_watch.body: The outlook improves if applications retain users, fees and liquidity after grants decline, and if validator ownership broadens while the client performs under adversarial shared-state load. It weakens if TVL follows rewards out, unlocks overwhelm demand or outages expose correlated software. Watch ninety- and 180-day application cohorts, stablecoin net flows, fees, base-fee burn versus issuance, actual unlocks, validator ownership and production incident history.

what_it_is.body: OP Mainnet is the original OP Stack Ethereum Layer 2. A Foundation-operated sequencer orders transactions, data is posted to Ethereum and fault proofs let participants challenge incorrect state proposals. OP Mainnet is one chain inside the wider Superchain. Base and other OP Chains are separate networks, so their activity must not be counted as OP Mainnet activity.

what_happened.body: OP Mainnet remains a mature, busy rollup, but its own capital and token are far below peak. TVL was $306.75 million, down 73.22% from August 2022, with $442.57 million of dollar stablecoins and $603.86 million of thirty-day DEX volume. OP traded near $0.087, 98.20% below its high. L2BEAT classified the rollup Stage 1 and recorded about 1.54 million user operations in the latest day.

why_this_outcome.body: Optimism made its technology easy for other chains to adopt. That succeeded: the OP Stack became widely distributed and OP Mainnet gained Ethereum-aligned tooling and security improvements. The same strategy weakened exclusivity. Better-distributed OP Chains can attract users and liquidity without those flows appearing on OP Mainnet. Because users pay ETH for gas and OP mainly governs the Collective, stack adoption and OP Mainnet usage do not automatically create OP token demand.

strategic_choices.body: Optimism chose an Ethereum rollup, released the OP Stack under an open license and built the Superchain around shared standards rather than protecting one chain. It uses ETH for OP Mainnet gas, routes all OP Mainnet revenue to the Collective treasury and gives OP holders governance rights. Protocol upgrades pass through technical review and stakeholder veto, but the Foundation and Security Council still co-control live upgrade execution.

operating_model.body: The sequencer accepts and orders ordinary transactions, then submits compressed data to Ethereum. Users can force inclusion through Ethereum if the sequencer fails, with delay. Anyone with sufficient funds can propose and challenge state roots through fault proofs. Governance signals and vetoes changes, while a Foundation-and-Security-Council 2-of-2 structure holds actual upgrade authority and regular upgrades have no user exit window.

token_and_value_capture.body: ETH is the gas token and pays execution plus Ethereum data costs. OP was created for governance, with an initial supply of 4.29 billion. OP Mainnet sends all of its revenue to the Optimism Collective treasury, while other Superchain members contribute under a separate revenue-share policy. That can fund shared infrastructure, but it is not the same as an automatic legal or economic claim for OP holders.

counterfactual.body: Keeping the stack proprietary might have protected more OP Mainnet activity, but would likely have reduced adoption and the Collective’s infrastructure influence. Using OP for gas could create direct transaction demand while adding onboarding friction and weakening ETH alignment. Either choice might improve local capture at the cost of the broader platform strategy; neither guarantees retained applications or liquidity.

risks_and_unknowns.body: The main risks are a centralized sequencer, instant upgrade authority, no pre-upgrade exit window, liquidity fragmentation and unclear OP capture from Superchain growth. OP Mainnet aggregates must remain separate from Base and other OP Chains. We lack a complete public reconciliation from every chain’s fees to Collective revenue, and network volume alone cannot show retained users or the profitability of the shared stack.

lifecycle.body: OP Mainnet is mixed. It is a successful piece of Ethereum infrastructure with live fault proofs, Stage 1 maturity and substantial daily use. Its own TVL is still 73.22% below peak and OP is 98.20% below its high. The stack succeeded more clearly than the flagship chain or token. That is a strategic trade-off: Optimism gained platform distribution while giving up exclusive ownership of the activity it enabled.

outlook_and_watch.body: The outlook improves if OP Mainnet retains applications while shared-chain revenue grows, interoperation becomes useful and governance reduces upgrade-key dependence. It weakens if liquidity keeps migrating to other chains, revenue attribution remains opaque or centralized controls persist. Watch chain-by-chain revenue contributions, OP Mainnet users and fees, stablecoin flows, sequencer diversity, proof participation, upgrade delays and OP governance participation.

what_it_is.body: Sui is a delegated-proof-of-stake Layer 1 built around Move objects rather than Ethereum accounts. Assets and application state can be owned, shared, immutable or wrapped. Independent owned-object transactions can avoid unnecessary global ordering, while shared objects use consensus. This design is not EVM compatible; developers adopt Sui Move and its object model to gain the concurrency and ownership benefits.

what_happened.body: Sui built a meaningful DeFi economy, then lost most of its peak capital. TVL was $414.70 million, down 84.27% from October 2025, with $429.47 million of dollar stablecoins and $791.93 million of thirty-day DEX volume. SUI traded near $0.691, 87.08% below its high. Reliability also became part of the story: an official report documented a January 2026 stall, then three more halts on May 28 and 29 after a major release.

why_this_outcome.body: Sui’s object model gives asset-heavy applications a real technical reason to use the chain, and first-party infrastructure helped turn that architecture into wallets, trading, storage and consumer products. The trade-off is a novel stack that must earn its own developers and liquidity while maturing in production. Large token reserves and affiliated support accelerated growth, but deep drawdowns and repeated halts show that technical differentiation did not yet create durable capital or reliability.

strategic_choices.body: Mysten Labs rejected EVM compatibility and designed Sui Move around assets as objects. The network separates independent object execution from shared-state consensus and uses delegated stake to choose validators. The Foundation also controls a large reserve released over time for builders, validators and distribution. During the May incident, the team knowingly used a fast interim fix with a small halt risk to restore service while a longer-term solution was built.

operating_model.body: A stake-weighted validator committee operates in epochs. SUI holders delegate to validators, and stake controls voting power. Transactions over independent owned objects can be processed without ordering every other transaction, while shared objects require consensus. Validators execute and certify state, and upgrades require coordinated software adoption. Mysten Labs develops core software; the Sui Foundation manages major ecosystem and token allocations.

token_and_value_capture.body: SUI pays gas, is delegated to validators, supplies onchain liquidity and carries governance rights. Supply is capped at 10 billion, but only about 5% circulated at mainnet launch and the Foundation can adjust releases to network needs. Storage fees enter a fund whose stake rewards compensate future validators, while deleting stored data creates rebates. This links use to SUI demand, but scheduled releases can still outrun activity.

counterfactual.body: EVM compatibility could have lowered developer and liquidity switching costs, but it would have surrendered much of Sui’s object-model differentiation. A narrower Foundation role could reduce dependency and attribution concerns while slowing ecosystem bootstrapping. More conservative upgrade sequencing or stronger failure containment might have reduced the 2026 halts, though the postmortems do not quantify the performance or delivery cost.

risks_and_unknowns.body: The leading risks are validator and Foundation stake concentration, future token releases, a novel execution stack, application exploits and repeat liveness failures. Volume does not show whether users return or whether incentives paid for the activity. We lack an independent beneficial-owner map for stake, an attributable split between affiliated and independent applications, and verified evidence that the January and May failure modes are fully contained.

lifecycle.body: Sui is mixed. It has a differentiated architecture, more than $400 million each of TVL and stablecoins, and nearly $792 million of thirty-day DEX volume. The 84.27% TVL drawdown, 87.08% token drawdown and four documented 2026 liveness incidents prevent a thriving call. The chain is useful and still developing, but it has not yet converted technical leadership into stable capital and reliability.

outlook_and_watch.body: The outlook improves if Sui runs for a sustained period without correlated halts, independent applications retain users and fees, and token releases become more transparent and broadly distributed. It weakens if another malformed input or restart-state bug halts the network, capital keeps leaving or incentives dominate use. Watch uptime, incident blast radius, validator ownership, release changes, TVL, stablecoin flows, application fees and ninety-day user retention.

what_it_is.body: NEAR is a sharded proof-of-stake Layer 1 with a WebAssembly runtime, named accounts and asynchronous receipts. Nightshade divides state and execution across shards while validators produce blocks, chunks and attestations. The current strategy extends beyond native applications: Chain Signatures and Intents let NEAR accounts coordinate transactions on external chains. Those external transactions are not automatically NEAR L1 activity.

what_happened.body: NEAR’s native capital remains far below its 2022 peak even as provider-tracked trading is high. TVL was $59.06 million, down 87.74%, with $65.11 million of dollar stablecoins and $2.53 billion of thirty-day DEX volume. That volume is unusually large relative to TVL and must be treated as a provider aggregate, not proof of unique users or native liquidity. NEAR traded at $1.74, 91.48% below its high.

why_this_outcome.body: NEAR first competed as a developer-friendly sharded L1, but Ethereum and Solana accumulated larger liquidity and application networks. It then reframed chain fragmentation as the product problem, using Intents and Chain Signatures to reach assets and users without requiring them to stay on NEAR. That creates a differentiated routing surface and helps explain high tracked volume, while making success harder to attribute: liquidity, execution and value can remain on other chains.

strategic_choices.body: NEAR chose sharding and a WebAssembly runtime rather than EVM compatibility, then built account abstraction, Intents and MPC-based Chain Signatures to reach other chains. Its newer AI and confidential-compute narrative adds a private shard operated by seven permissioned validators and connected through a TEE bridge. That private service is separate from public NEAR mainnet and should not be presented as the security model of the public chain.

operating_model.body: Validators stake NEAR and rotate through roles producing blocks, chunks and chunk attestations. Normal validator work is assigned across shards, while the runtime executes Wasm contracts and routes asynchronous receipts. Chain Signatures use a separate MPC operator network to create signatures for external chains; clients still broadcast and settle those transactions on the destination network. Cross-chain products therefore add solver, MPC, relayer and external-chain dependencies.

token_and_value_capture.body: NEAR pays gas and storage, is staked for security and rewards validators. The current validator documentation targets annual rewards equal to 2.5% of total supply. Transaction fees burn after the contract rebate, and contracts receive 30% of their generated gas fees. Cross-chain product volume does not automatically mean the same amount of NEAR is bought or burned, so Intents economics require separate, reproducible accounting.

counterfactual.body: Staying focused on native applications could have produced simpler attribution, but would force NEAR to compete directly with larger chain ecosystems for every user and dollar of liquidity. EVM compatibility might reduce switching costs while sacrificing parts of the Wasm and sharding design. A bridge-only strategy would be easier to reason about than Intents and MPC signing, but would not offer the same programmable cross-chain account layer.

risks_and_unknowns.body: The main risks are thin native liquidity, solver or MPC concentration, external-chain and bridge failures, unclear token capture and narrative dependence on AI. The seven-validator private shard must never be conflated with public mainnet. We lack independent attribution for the large DEX-volume figure, an entity map for cross-chain operators, and a reconciled statement showing what cross-chain fees become NEAR burns, buybacks or treasury revenue.

lifecycle.body: Near is mixed. The network is live, sharded and still producing more than $3.15 million of thirty-day fees, while tracked DEX volume is large. Native TVL is 87.74% below peak and NEAR is 91.48% below its high. Chain abstraction gives the project a credible second act, but the current data does not prove that routed activity creates a durable moat, retained native capital or sufficient token value capture.

outlook_and_watch.body: The outlook improves if independently measured cross-chain use repeats, solver and MPC control broadens, and fees reconcile to NEAR burns or other enforceable capture while native liquidity stabilizes. It weakens if routed volume is concentrated, subsidized or captured elsewhere. Watch native TVL and stablecoins, Intents and DEX attribution, retained users, solver concentration, MPC thresholds, fee-to-token reconciliation and adoption outside first-party AI demonstrations.

what_it_is.body: Mantle is an EVM-compatible Ethereum Layer 2 that now posts transaction data to Ethereum blobs and uses OP Succinct validity proofs for state updates. A centralized sequencer orders transactions, and MNT is the gas asset. This report covers Mantle Network only. Mantle treasury, mETH and other affiliated products are separate entities and their assets must not be counted as network TVL or revenue unless a provider explicitly does so.

what_happened.body: Mantle repeatedly changed its technical stack while retaining a live ecosystem. OP Succinct went live in September 2025, and the April 16, 2026 Arsia upgrade removed EigenDA so data now sits on Ethereum. TVL was $68.20 million, down 90.32% from its April 16 peak, while dollar stablecoins were $576.56 million. Thirty-day DEX volume rose 629.17% from a small prior base. MNT traded near $0.396, 86.12% below its high.

why_this_outcome.body: Mantle combined EVM familiarity, MNT gas and governance-linked capital to seed liquidity in a crowded L2 market. It then improved the security story by moving data to Ethereum and state validation to ZK proofs. Those upgrades did not by themselves create a distribution moat. Base and other L2s have stronger user funnels, while Mantle’s treasury and affiliated products can make the brand look larger than the network. Incentive-responsive capital explains a high peak without proving retained applications.

strategic_choices.body: Mantle chose an Ethereum L2 with MNT as gas, funded ecosystem expansion through tokenholder governance and kept a modular architecture that could replace major components. It migrated from EigenDA to Ethereum blobs and from optimistic validation toward OP Succinct proofs. Governance can direct products, treasury and architecture through MIPs, but most implementation remains offchain. These choices enable fast coordinated pivots while preserving concentrated execution and upgrade power.

operating_model.body: Users send EVM transactions to the sequencer, which orders blocks and batches compressed data into Ethereum blobs. A permissioned proposer submits OP Succinct proofs and state roots to Ethereum. Users can force transactions through L1 after delay if the sequencer fails, but withdrawals depend on new state roots. L2BEAT classifies Mantle Stage 0; contracts can be upgraded without a user exit window and multiple multisigs retain material control.

token_and_value_capture.body: MNT pays execution, Ethereum data and operator fees on Mantle. Tokenholders vote on MIPs that can direct treasury spending, products and technical choices. Gas use creates MNT demand, but the reviewed sources do not establish that holders own a legal claim on the treasury, mETH revenue or affiliated businesses. Network fees were $1.79 million over thirty days and provider-reported protocol revenue was $246,011, not net income.

counterfactual.body: Using ETH for gas could simplify onboarding and Ethereum comparability, while reducing direct MNT utility. Moving to Ethereum data earlier might have improved the security story but raised costs during the bootstrapping period. Smaller, milestone-based incentives could produce cleaner evidence of retained demand, while slowing ecosystem growth. None of these choices would create a user funnel or category-defining application on its own.

risks_and_unknowns.body: The largest risks are centralized sequencing, permissioned proposing, instant upgrades, proof-system or verifier failure, treasury concentration, token price reflexivity and weak local distribution. The 629% volume change is a low-base signal, not proof of a durable surge. We lack clean attribution between network and affiliated-product economics, a subsidy-adjusted application cohort and a public beneficial-owner map for controlling multisigs.

lifecycle.body: Mantle is mixed. It is an operating rollup with Ethereum data, ZK proofs, more than $576 million of stablecoins and a recent burst of trading. TVL is still 90.32% below peak, MNT is 86.12% below its high and Stage 0 controls remain. The architecture is materially better than the early design, but the chain has not yet shown that security upgrades and treasury resources translate into retained local demand.

outlook_and_watch.body: The outlook improves if applications retain users and fees after incentives, TVL stabilizes, governance adds upgrade delays and permissionless proposing, and MNT fee demand grows without relying on affiliated balance sheets. It weakens if volume fades, capital keeps leaving or a centralized control fails. Watch application cohorts, stablecoin net flows, fees and revenue, MNT gas demand, treasury deployment, proposer liveness, proof verification and Stage 1 progress.
